article_title: Utilisation of SWOT Analysis for Decision-Making in Educational Contexts
citation: Keravnos, N., & Orphanos, S. (2025). Utilisation of SWOT analysis for decision-making in educational contexts. European Journal of Educational Management, 8(4), 219-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/eujem.8.4.219
title: Four-phase cyclical SWOT routine: diagnose, prioritise, implement, review and re-cycle
description: The CSM-SU organises strategic SWOT use into four interconnected, recurring phases: (1) Engage and Diagnose with multi-source internal and external data; (2) Interpret and Prioritise organisational interactions; (3) Develop and Implement actionable plans through distributed leadership; and (4) Review, Learn, and Re-Cycle insights. The updated SWOT profile "feeds directly back into Phase 1, triggering a new—and now more informed—cycle of diagnosis", embodying the feedback loops of open-systems theory. Each phase includes decision points allowing teams to customise activities to local circumstances.
requirements: Scheduled intervals at which the SWOT team reconvenes to review progress and update the SWOT profile
constraints: Schools vary in size, development stage, and community context, so phases must be adapted to local circumstances
target_learners: School leadership teams
Teachers, support staff, parents, and students participating in strategic analysis
target_learning_goals: Organisational learning
Strategic planning and adaptive school improvement
examples: Phase 1 combines quantitative data (achievement trends, attendance, budget) with qualitative sources (observations, interviews, climate indicators) and a simplified PEST scan to build a preliminary SWOT profile
key_sources: Keravnos, N., & Orphanos, S. (2025). Utilisation of SWOT analysis for decision-making in educational contexts. European Journal of Educational Management, 8(4), 219-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/eujem.8.4.219

article_title: Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom
citation: Peter Fowles, Erik Falor, Sulove Bhattarai, John Edwards, and Seth Poulsen. (2026). Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21374
title: CS1-CR course structure: unrestricted AI use with mandatory oral code review interviews and a flipped classroom
description: CS1-CR is a CS1 course design in which students may freely use generative AI on coding assignments but must complete "an oral, in-person code review (CR) interview session with a TA or instructor within 48 hours after each submission deadline". Rubric scores count for 30% of the assignment grade and code review performance for 70%, with a zero for missing the session. One of three weekly class days was cancelled for interviews, replaced by a flipped classroom with pre-class lecture videos and in-class coding activities. Eleven TAs were trained via mock interviews and structured per-assignment interview protocols.
requirements: Trained TAs with a structured per-assignment interview protocol
Scheduling infrastructure (tutoring center app) and a free weekly class day for interview sessions
constraints: Adds extra student-TA contact time, making truly controlled studies difficult
Scaling beyond about 100 students with the same number of TAs is untested
target_learners: University introductory computer science (CS1) students
target_learning_goals: Understanding and justifying submitted code
Core programming concepts such as Python syntax, logic, tracing, and functions
examples: In Fall 2025, 96 students completed weekly 15-minute code review interviews after each assignment submission with no restrictions on AI tool usage.
key_sources: Peter Fowles, Erik Falor, Sulove Bhattarai, John Edwards, and Seth Poulsen. (2026). Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21374

article_title: CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming
citation: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench
title: CSTutorBench: a 17-question benchmark with an 8-criterion pedagogical rubric for evaluating LLMs as VEX VR block-based programming tutors
description: CSTutorBench is a benchmark for evaluating language models as CS tutors in VEX VR, a block-based robotics simulation for middle school students. It contains 17 scenario-based questions across four types (debugging, debugging_iterative, optimization, conceptual), each scored on an 8-criterion rubric (0–2 points each, 16 points max) with universal and type-specific criteria, plus evaluator notes hidden from the model under test. The rubric "operationalizes established research on tutoring and formative feedback into computable dimensions," and the benchmark, rubric, and full evaluation pipeline are released on GitHub.
requirements: Requires a human-in-the-loop LLM-as-judge evaluation pipeline with per-question hybrid review and calibration notes carried forward across questions
constraints: The evaluation set contains only 17 questions, which the authors state limits the precision of per-criterion comparisons; type-specific criteria are scored on subsets as small as one or two questions
All items are single-turn and do not capture multi-turn tutoring dialogues; models have not been evaluated with actual students, so higher rubric scores may not predict learning outcomes
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8) working in block-based programming environments
target_learning_goals: block-based programming in VEX VR, including sequencing, sensor navigation, and algorithmic optimization
examples: The six debugging_iterative entries approximate multi-turn tutoring by presenting 2–3 code snapshots of a student's self-directed fix attempts, such as a student who first tries a repeat-10 loop then switches to repeat-100
key_sources: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench

article_title: CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming
citation: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench
title: CSTutorBench rubric operationalizes tutoring and formative-feedback research into eight computable scoring criteria
description: The rubric translates established tutoring and feedback research into eight scored criteria (0–2 points each): seven universal criteria plus one type-specific criterion per question type. Conciseness reflects Shute's finding that "feedback complexity is inversely related to error correction and learning efficiency"; Actionability draws on Hattie and Timperley's model of feedback that reduces the gap between current and desired performance; Targetedness is grounded in expert human tutors who engage with specific contextual factors rather than generic advice. The four type-specific criteria reflect Narciss's interactive tutoring feedback (ITF) model, which holds that no single feedback type is optimal across all tasks and feedback must be calibrated to both the task and the student's state.
requirements: Each criterion includes a stable description across entries plus entry-specific addenda describing correct and incorrect responses, to maintain consistency while capturing domain knowledge
constraints: The type-specific criteria each apply only to their question type (e.g., hint not solution on the 8 debugging questions, acknowledges progression on the 6 iterative debugging questions)
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8)
target_learning_goals: receiving effective tutoring and formative feedback in block-based programming
examples: The acknowledges_progression criterion specifically evaluates whether a response recognizes and builds on the student's prior fix attempts provided as context
key_sources: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench

article_title: Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency
citation: Shangchao Min, Shaonan Wang, Xinyu Gao, Hui Wang, Zhiling Jin, and 2 more. (2026). Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8820245/v1
title: CSEBench: a CSE-aligned benchmark of 624 expert-annotated multiple-choice items with human response data
description: CSEBench is a publicly released benchmark for assessing LLM English proficiency against China's Standards of English Language Ability. It comprises "624 expert-annotated multiple-choice questions spanning CSE Levels 2–7", each annotated with CSE difficulty level, one of four target subskills (vocabulary, syntax, phonology, cohesion/discourse), student level, sublabels, average accuracy, and discrimination. Items come from two diagnostic forms (junior-high, 39 items; college, 35 items) linked by 13 anchor items, with responses from 2,050 Chinese EFL learners. The dataset is publicly available on OSF.
requirements: Items require expert annotation of CSE difficulty level and subskill, plus IRT-estimated difficulty from human response data for calibration
constraints: Spans only CSE Levels 2–7, producing ceiling effects for frontier closed-source models
Does not capture productive skills such as speaking and writing, nor interactional competence or pragmatic appropriateness
target_learners: Chinese EFL learners in Grade 8 and college sophomore cohorts
target_learning_goals: English proficiency assessment across vocabulary, syntax, phonology, and cohesion/discourse subskills
examples: Two large-scale diagnostic forms were assembled from an existing item bank: a junior-high form with 39 items and a college form with 35 items, sharing 13 anchor items for linking
key_sources: Shangchao Min, Shaonan Wang, Xinyu Gao, Hui Wang, Zhiling Jin, and 2 more. (2026). Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8820245/v1

article_title: Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency
citation: Shangchao Min, Shaonan Wang, Xinyu Gao, Hui Wang, Zhiling Jin, and 2 more. (2026). Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8820245/v1
title: Psychometric pipeline for mapping LLM performance onto interpretable proficiency levels and subskill mastery
description: The article's organizing framework integrates educational measurement methods into LLM evaluation: "we estimate item difficulty using a two-parameter logistic (2PL) item response theory (IRT) model fitted to responses from 2,050 Chinese EFL learners", then conduct a Bookmark standard-setting study with trained experts to establish cut scores for CSE Levels 3–6, and finally perform cognitive diagnosis using an expert-defined Q-matrix with higher-order cognitive diagnosis models selected by fit (HO-GDINA won). This yields scale-referenced proficiency levels and subskill mastery probabilities rather than raw accuracy, enabling educationally meaningful interpretation of model ability.
requirements: Human response data for item calibration
Expert standard-setting panel familiar with CSE descriptors
Expert-defined Q-matrix mapping items to attributes
constraints: The item bank contains few CSE-7 items, limiting reliable claims about proficiency above CSE-6
Proficiency estimates may vary with prompt design, exemplar selection, or formatting
target_learners: LLMs evaluated as simulated language users, calibrated against Chinese EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Proficiency-level reporting and subskill diagnosis for English language ability
examples: The Bookmark standard-setting session involved panelist training, then two rounds of judgments, with Round 2 placements used as final cut scores for CSE Levels 3–6

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: CSCL processes operate at individual, small-group, and classroom levels that interpenetrate without being reducible
description: The editorial argues that CSCL settings involve processes — "cognitive, knowledge-building, interactional, or identity-forming" — at the small-group and/or classroom level as well as the individual student level. These "Processes at these different levels interpenetrate with each other intimately, without being reducible to any one level". CSCL additionally mediates learning, interaction, and cognition by technological artifacts and computational media, so researchers need more elaborated theories and methods to capture these processes and mediations.
requirements: Theories and methods elaborated enough to capture multiple levels of description and their technological mediations
constraints: Traditional training sciences focus on the individual learner, with culture conceived only at a broad societal level
target_learners: CSCL researchers and practitioners implementing CSCL in practice
target_learning_goals: Understanding collaborative learning as multi-level, artifact-mediated interaction
examples: The issue's articles each focus on different levels and their special mediations, proposing new ways of viewing what takes place there.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: CSCL pluralism: the field advances through confrontation and critique of multiple paradigms
description: The editorial's organizing framework holds that CSCL, as a multi-disciplinary field with inherently multifaceted goals, should foster an ecology of competing theoretical, methodological, pedagogical and technological perspectives rather than converge on one approach. The authors write that "Scientific revolutions — like political revolutions — advance through the confrontation of viewpoints and the critique of established paradigms," and argue that dominant positions "restrict innovative thinking and practices." ijCSCL is positioned as a venue for dialog among alternative perspectives.
requirements: A venue that publishes and juxtaposes alternative paradigms so viewpoints can be confronted and critiqued
constraints: The authors frame this as a stance for the research field, not a tested empirical result
target_learners: CSCL researchers and the learning sciences community
target_learning_goals: Advancing theory-building and research practice in computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The issue pairs counter-poised papers on theory, analysis, and technology so contrasting approaches are presented side by side
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8

article_title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
citation: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6
title: Design CSCL visualization and argumentation tools so externalized group work frees the teacher from task structuring to scaffold by increasing challenge
description: Because the interactive whiteboard records and shares all subgroups' contributions, the teacher gains a broadened basis for informed classroom scaffolding and spends less time providing cognitive assistance and structuring the task. The article concludes that such tools "mediate the teachers scaffolding by freeing up their time to extend student abilities with greater challenges based on the shared problem-solving space of the group rather than scaffold the rules of the activity." Appropriate scaffolding still depends on the teacher's domain knowledge and pedagogy experience.
requirements: Technology that provides a visual record of what students understood and shared across subgroups
A teacher with domain knowledge and pedagogy experience to select among expanded scaffolding choices
constraints: The finding is from a case study of one expert teacher (30 years of clinical and teaching experience) blinded to the research questions, in a medical training context
target_learners: small-group collaborative learners in medical PBL
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
adaptive problem-solving behavior
examples: In the IW condition the teacher created scaffolding strategies based on what was recorded and shared by all subgroups, and the nurse talked less than in the TW group

article_title: Reigniting CSCL flash themes
citation: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse. (2013). Reigniting CSCL flash themes. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:369–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9185-0
title: CSCL research must remain centrally concerned with meaning making in joint activity, however technological the theme or objective the methodology
description: The editors conclude that no matter how technological the theme and no matter how objective the methodology, issues of human group meaning making must still be centrally addressed in CSCL. They invoke Koschmann's formulation that the field must be "centrally concerned with meaning and the practices of meaning making in the context of joint activity, and the ways in which these practices are mediated through designed artifacts." This principle orients evaluation of all four flash themes, from gaze indicators to learning-analytics visualizations.
requirements: Research designs must connect objective interaction data to intersubjective meaning making
target_learners: CSCL researchers and educational designers
target_learning_goals: collaborative meaning making
intersubjectivity
examples: The editors apply this principle critically to each study: gaze data must be tied to meaning making, argument quality is an attribute of group interaction, and abstract analytics representations raise the question of how participants make sense of them.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse. (2013). Reigniting CSCL flash themes. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:369–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9185-0

article_title: What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations?
citation: van Leeuwen, A., Rummel, N., & van Gog, T. (2019). What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 14, 261–289. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09299-x
title: Three levels of interpretational aid in CSCL teacher dashboards: mirroring, alerting, and advising
description: Building on Soller et al.'s algorithm for collaboration support tools, the article distinguishes dashboards by which agent - tool or teacher - performs detection and interpretation. "Mirroring dashboards" display analyzed data for the teacher to peruse at will; "alerting" dashboards additionally flag groups deviating from a standard; "advising" dashboards "not only display information and alert to certain events, but also assist in the interpretation" by providing advice about what is happening or what action to take. This typology structures the three experimental conditions.
requirements: Alerting and advising require comparing group status to some standard to detect events
Advising requires the system to generate advice referencing the dashboard's indicators
constraints: The article found only one prior example of an advising dashboard in CSCL (Chen 2006), so higher levels of aid are scarcely studied
target_learners: Primary school teachers
Pre-service primary school teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher monitoring of collaborating students and decisions about support
examples: The experiment instantiated the three levels as three versions of one prototype: information alone, information plus alerts, and information plus alerts plus advisory prompts

citation: Michael J. Baker, Peter Reimann. (2024). CSCL has come of age. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2024) 19:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09419-2
title: CSCL's triadic object of study: collaboration, task, and technology
description: The editors characterize CSCL research as organized around an integrated, three-part object of study. As they state, "CSCL research is characterised by the three-fold nature of its integrated object of study: collaboration, with respect to a more or less shared task, involving use of technology." Each of the three terms is theory-laden (e.g. 'task' can be a problem solving goal, a learning object, or the object of activity), a change in one element has repercussions for the others, and the object evolves with society and its technologies. The editorial uses this framework to survey what is currently emerging in CSCL research across all three elements.
requirements: The framework presupposes treating the three elements as interdependent rather than separately studied
constraints: The editorial notes that none of the three key terms is neutral and each is highly theory-laden

citation: Zhou, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Ryan, Z., Stiso, C., Murphy, D., Danish, J., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G. (2025). Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09438-z
title: Design CSCL environments that explicitly cultivate social norms and epistemic goals so students can manage disagreement productively
description: The article argues that productive disagreement in peer critique depends on an environment where students feel safe disagreeing and view disagreement as a path to better knowledge. It states it is "essential to cultivate a CSCL environment where students feel confident and comfortable about managing disagreement," and that "creating such an environment requires intentional development of shared goals and social norms." Norms such as building on ideas, accountability to each other, supporting ideas with reasons, and consensus-building should be established so disagreements become opportunities to construct more accurate scientific knowledge rather than sources of conflict.
